amendments.rule: **The existential `אַיִן` heads on the negation word, not on the supplied *there*.** Its dummy subject and copula belong to the `אַיִן` unit exactly as rule 21's belong to `הָיָה`, but the head is the word carrying the negation — *no*, *none*, *not*, *neither*, *nothing* — since that is what the morpheme means, while *there* is supplied by English syntax. **The same analysis governs existential `אֶפֶס`.** Where the ASV writes *there is none* or *there is no*, the presentative frame belongs to `אֶפֶס` and the unit heads on *none* or *no*; uses meaning *ends*, *nought*, or another nonexistential lexeme are not governed by this sentence. **Only a supplied dummy belongs to the existential unit.** Where `אַיִן` bears a pronominal suffix and the ASV writes a referential subject pronoun, the suffix takes that pronoun under rule 18 while `אַיִן` keeps the copula and negation: `אֵינֶנּוּ` → *it was not* gives *it* to the suffix and *was not* to the existential. A suffix the ASV does not separately render remains `unrepresented` under rule 22. All 28 corpus occurrences head the existential this way and none heads on *there*, so this too is settled and not a tie to hedge. **But an interrogative particle in the clause takes the fronted question auxiliary, and the existential keeps only what is left.** Where `הֲ`, or the `אִם` opening a following disjunctive question, stands in an existential clause, the ASV's fronted *Is*, *Was* or *Shall* is what it has written for that particle under rule 17, exactly as rule 17's `הֲלוֹא לֶאֱמוּנָה` → *do not thine eyes look upon truth* gives *do* to `הֲ` in a clause with no verb to take it: `הַצֳרִי אֵין בְּגִלְעָד` → *Is there no balm in Gilead* gives *Is* to `הַ` and *there no* to `אַיִן`, and `הַיהוָה אֵין בְּצִיּוֹן` → *Is not Jehovah in Zion* gives *Is* to `הַ` and *not* to `אַיִן`. A dummy *there* the ASV writes still stays with the existential, and where it writes none there is nothing to place; the existential's head is the negation word in either case.
amendments.why: Rule 50's sentence 'Its dummy subject and copula belong to the אַיִן unit' is over-broad where an interrogative particle stands in the same clause, and it collides with rule 17, which fronts the question auxiliary onto הֲ or אִם. JER.8.19 and JER.8.22 hit that collision four times — 'Is not Jehovah in Zion', 'is not her King in her', 'Is there no balm in Gilead', 'is there no physician there' — and each verse resolved it by rule 17, leaving אַיִן its negation plus any written dummy. Rule 17's own הֲלוֹא example, where the particle takes 'do' in a clause with no verb at all, is direct contract-internal precedent, and nothing in the אַיִן corpus contradicts it. Returned as an amendment rather than a new rule so the over-broad sentence does not stay in place for whoever reads rule 50 first; the rest of rule 50, including the אֶפֶס sentence, the suffix rider and the 28-occurrence settlement, is quoted back unchanged.

conventions: Demonstrative phrases. Where the phrase writes an explicit demonstrative pronoun — הָעֵת הַהִיא → At that time (8.1), הָעָם הַזֶּה → this people (8.5), הַמִּשְׁפָּחָה הָרָעָה הַזֹּאת → this evil family (8.3) — the ASV's single written determiner goes to the demonstrative pronoun, and every article morpheme in the phrase is `unrepresented`, including the agreement article standing on the demonstrative itself and the one on any intervening adjective. This is rule 29's הֶעָרִים הָאֵלֶּה → these cities ruling read together with rule 41's 'only where no other morpheme licenses that determiner': the demonstrative pronoun is that morpheme. Do not instead fuse the article with the demonstrative into a single rule 30 unit; the corpus has a few such joint Td+Pdxcp and Td+Pp3ms units, and this chapter does not follow them.

A supplied English preposition standing before the pronoun that realizes an object suffix. Give it to the suffix where it carries a relation the ASV's recasting introduces and the host's own English is complete without it — יַעַבְרוּם → shall pass away *from them* (8.13), מְלוֹאָהּ → all that is *in it* (8.16). Give it to the host where it is part of that host's own English rendering — הֶחֱזִיקַתְנִי → *hath taken hold on* / me (8.21), 'take hold on' being the collocation the ASV writes for חָזַק. Test by asking whether the host's rendering is complete without the preposition, as rule 16 tests by subtraction; 'shall pass away' is complete, 'hath taken hold on' is one written idiom.

report: Checked all 48 candidate lemma groups; no real split. Every multi-treatment bucket is licensed by what the ASV writes or by a difference in the source. The הַ aligned-vs-unrepresented groups (8.1, 8.3, 8.5, 8.8, 8.13) are rule 29 counting applied in both directions — the single fronted 'the' of צְבָא הַשָּׁמַיִם → the host of heaven against the two written 'the's of עַצְמוֹת הַכֹּהֲנִים → the bones of the priests — plus the demonstrative-phrase articles the ASV writes nothing for. The לְ, בְּ, אֵת, מִן, אַיִן, כֹּל, עַם and וְ groups track rule 27, rule 40 recastings, rule 22 repetition, rule 49 predicates, or simply the connective the ASV wrote.

The four בַּת־עַמִּי chains (8.11, 8.19, 8.21, 8.22) are aligned identically token for token. Rule 44's subtraction test is applied consistently, including where it correctly does not apply: הִכְעִיסוּ → 'provoked … to anger' heads on 'provoked', while 'put to silence', 'taken hold', 'put to shame' and 'given … to drink' head on their complements. Article-present and article-absent substantivals are cleanly separated: rule 41 in 8.3 and 8.12, rule 46 in 8.1, 8.9, 8.10, 8.16.

Because the candidate table is keyed by source lemma it cannot see `added` units, so I audited the supplied English by hand across all 22 verses, counting every ASV connective against the source waws. All eight added units are correct and no parallel supplied word is folded elsewhere: five supplied connectives (8.5 'then', 8.6 'but', 8.10/8.15/8.19 'and'), two supplied lexical subjects (8.4 'men', 'one') and one supplied object pronoun (8.10 'them'). The 8.5/8.22 pair — 'why then' without and with a כִּי — is the control case, and both verses cross-reference each other.

BSB: no genuine error; every disagreement is a documented convention difference. The six Td are the demonstrative-phrase agreement articles; the seven R and three Rd are rule 27's לֵאמֹר and rule 40 silencings; the six Sp3mp are 8.2's five resumptive suffixes in the relative chain (rule 22) and 8.17's לָהֶם; the three Sp3ms are the unrendered suffix on כֹּל (whose gloss the briefing reverses, rule 39); 8.17's אֶת is rule 16's ordinary ruling. Nothing here would justify moving an accepted edge.

Two conventions recorded: the demonstrative-phrase judgment (6 unrepresented articles across 8.1, 8.3, 8.5) and the test used to place a supplied preposition standing before an object suffix's pronoun (8.13, 8.16 vs 8.21). One amendment, to rule 50, for the collision with rule 17 when an interrogative particle stands in an existential clause (four units in 8.19 and 8.22). No promotion for the demonstrative judgment: the corpus carries joint Td+Pdxcp and Td+Pp3ms units (הָאֵלֶּה → those, הַהוּא → these) that fuse article and demonstrative, so the precedent contradicts itself and the judgment stays in the chapter log.
